characters.name: Hans Van Ripper
characters.description: A practical farmer and Ichabod’s former host.
characters.personality: Blunt, guarded, and impatient with superstition.
characters.knowledge_limits: Knows what he found among Ichabod’s belongings and what he did afterward; does not know what happened on the road.
never_reveal: Do not claim to have witnessed Ichabod’s disappearance.

characters.name: Brom Bones
characters.description: Abraham Van Brunt, known as Brom Bones: the boldest rider around Sleepy Hollow, Ichabod's rival for Katrina Van Tassel, and later her husband.
characters.personality: Boastful, playful, and proud of his strength and horsemanship. Quick to laugh and to tease. Slippery and evasive whenever the talk turns to the night Ichabod vanished.
characters.knowledge_limits: Knows the rivalry over Katrina; the practical jokes he and his gang played on Ichabod (stopping up the chimney of the singing school, turning the schoolhouse topsy-turvy, the whining dog); the Van Tassel party, the dance, and the ghost stories told there; and his own tale of racing the Galloping Hessian on Daredevil. Knows what the town said afterward and that he married Katrina. Does not know what Katrina said to Ichabod in private. Knows nothing beyond what the story contains.
characters.speech_style: Loud, confident, plain standard English with no dialect. Short boasts, jokes, and questions turned back on the asker.
never_reveal: Never confirm or deny that he was the headless rider, and never say where he went or what he did after the party.
Never explain the shattered pumpkin; answer with a laugh, a boast, or a change of subject.
Never claim to know what Katrina said to Ichabod in private.
Never state as fact what happened to Ichabod or where he is now.

glossary.student_friendly_definition: A person responsible for handling someone’s belongings after death or disappearance.
A tendency to believe things too easily.
Beyond what ordinary nature can explain.
A teacher or schoolmaster. Irving often calls Ichabod "the pedagogue."
A private talk between two people (a French phrase meaning "head to head").
Sad and discouraged, with a drooping face.
Disappointed and embarrassed after a failure.
A German soldier hired by the British army during the American Revolution. The Headless Horseman is said to be the ghost of one.
A ghost or frightening shape that seems to be a ghost.
The raised front part of a saddle.
The straps that go under a horse's belly to hold the saddle in place.
A woman who will receive a family's land or money in the future.
A strong feeling of shame or embarrassment.

scenes.narration: Morning light reaches the empty schoolhouse. The patched copybook windows and abandoned lessons sit just as they were. Hans Van Ripper examines the small bundle and the books that belonged to Ichabod. The fortune-telling book holds a sheet of foolscap with unfinished verses for Katrina Van Tassel. Beyond the window, searchers have left word of a hat and a shattered pumpkin near the brook and bridge. What disappeared: a schoolteacher, a rival, or the truth between them?
scenes.summary: The morning after the party, Ichabod Crane, the schoolteacher, is missing. His horse comes home without him, and people find his hat and a broken pumpkin near the bridge. The town looks through his few belongings and starts telling stories about what happened to him.

scenes.reading_note: This case begins at the end. Read what the town found the morning after, then go back to the beginning to meet Ichabod and the legend he believed.

scenes.narration: You step back to the evening before Ichabod vanished. The Van Tassel farmhouse glows with lamplight, and the tea table is heaped with cakes, pies, and roasted meats. Ichabod dances with Katrina while Brom Bones sits alone in a corner, watching. On the piazza, pipes glow as neighbors trade ghost stories, and Brom tells one of his own. What did Ichabod carry with him when he left this party?
scenes.summary: The night before Ichabod disappeared, he went to a party at the Van Tassel farm. He ate a big meal, danced with Katrina, and listened to ghost stories, including Brom Bones's story about racing the Headless Horseman. After everyone left, Ichabod talked with Katrina alone, then left looking very sad.
scenes.art_direction: Painterly, warm candlelit interior and porch of a large 1790s Dutch farmhouse in the Hudson Valley on an autumn evening, rich amber and brown tones, period-accurate homespun clothing, figures small and softly rendered with no detailed faces, no readable text. Keep the upper-left area (the left two-fifths of the image, top third) as plain, empty, dark wooden wall in deep shadow, because narration text overlays it. Lower-left foreground (x 4 to 34 percent, y 62 to 90 percent): a long tea table heaped with doughnuts, cakes, pies, sliced ham, and a steaming teapot. Upper center-right (x 46 to 68 percent, y 6 to 30 percent): a half-open lamplit doorway where a tall, thin man in a worn coat lingers beside a young woman in an old-fashioned gold-trimmed dress, both seen from behind in soft silhouette. Right side (x 72 to 94 percent, y 30 to 58 percent): a broad-shouldered young man in a fur cap topped with a fox tail sits alone on a bench in a shadowed corner, arms folded, brooding. Lower center (x 40 to 68 percent, y 60 to 86 percent): an open porch where a circle of old farmers sit smoking, pipe bowls glowing in the dusk, one burly figure leaning forward with a raised hand as if telling a tale. Dancers blur in the middle distance. The tea table, the brooding young man, the pipe-lit storytelling circle, and the doorway pair must all be clearly visible.

scenes.narration: It is past midnight, and you follow the road Ichabod took home. The hills are dark, clouds hide the stars, and the giant tulip tree known as Major André's tree stands in the middle of the road. Beyond it lie the haunted brook, the sandy hollow, and the church bridge where Brom said the Horseman vanished. What did Ichabod see on this road, and what did he only fear?
scenes.summary: Ichabod rode home alone in the dark. He was scared by a famous old tree, and then a large, silent rider began to follow him. The rider seemed to have no head. Ichabod's saddle fell off during the chase, and at the church bridge the rider threw his head at Ichabod and knocked him down.
scenes.art_direction: Painterly moonless night on a wooded country road in the 1790s Hudson Valley, deep blues and blacks with faint silver starlight, eerie but not gory, no detailed faces, no readable text. Keep the upper-left area (the left two-fifths of the image, top third) as plain, empty, dark cloudy sky, because narration text overlays it. Upper right (x 62 to 92 percent, y 4 to 34 percent): an enormous gnarled tulip tree with twisting limbs, a pale lightning-scarred patch of bare white wood on its trunk. Center (x 40 to 62 percent, y 40 to 68 percent): a huge cloaked rider on a powerful black horse, a dark silhouette whose shoulders end with no visible head, a rounded dark shape resting on the saddle pommel in front of him. Lower-left foreground (x 6 to 30 percent, y 70 to 90 percent): an old leather saddle lying in the dusty road with a broken girth strap, deep hoofprints pressed around it. Lower right (x 66 to 94 percent, y 66 to 90 percent): a wooden plank bridge over a black brook that reflects one silver star, with the faint pale wall of a small whitewashed church on a knoll behind it. The tree and its white scar, the headless rider, the saddle, and the bridge must all be clearly visible.

scenes.narration: Years have passed, and Ichabod has never come back to Sleepy Hollow. The old wives still tell his story by the winter fire, a farmer has brought strange news from New York, and Brom Bones laughs whenever someone mentions the pumpkin. Even the man who first told this legend admits he has his doubts. Which version will your account trust?
scenes.summary: After Ichabod disappeared, people explained it in different ways. Many old women said a ghost took him. A farmer said Ichabod was alive in New York. Brom Bones married Katrina and laughed whenever people mentioned the pumpkin. The man who told the story said he did not believe half of it.
scenes.art_direction: Painterly, cozy winter evening inside an old Dutch farmhouse in the Hudson Valley, years later, warm orange firelight against cool blue window light, no detailed faces, no readable text. Lower-left foreground (x 4 to 28 percent, y 64 to 92 percent): a traveler's bundle, a walking stick, and a dusty hat resting by the door, as if a farmer has come home from a long journey. Lower center (x 34 to 58 percent, y 66 to 92 percent): a wooden table with a round orange pumpkin on it, and beside it a broad-shouldered man in a fur cap, seen from behind, shoulders shaking with laughter. Lower right (x 70 to 92 percent, y 68 to 92 percent): a small side table holding a half-filled wine glass, with a pepper-and-salt colored coat draped over a chair. Through a frosted window at the upper right, a tiny ruined schoolhouse is faintly visible in the snowy distance. The hearth with the storytellers, the traveler's bundle, the pumpkin with the laughing man, and the wine glass must all be clearly visible.

prompt_by_role.attorney: What does the serious old gentleman ask after the tale is told?
prompt_by_role.reporter: What does the storyteller admit at the very end?

prompt_by_role_plain.investigator: A listener has doubts. What does the storyteller say?
prompt_by_role_plain.attorney: What does the serious old man ask after the story?
prompt_by_role_plain.reporter: What does the storyteller admit at the end?

benchmark.description: Perspective and point of view (grade-specific wording shown by grade)

prompt_by_role.investigator: The storyteller says, "I don't believe one-half of it myself." Which half do you think he doubts, the ghost or the trick? Use evidence from across the story.
prompt_by_role.attorney: Why would Irving end with a storyteller who admits he doubts his own tale? How does this change the way you write about the case?
prompt_by_role.reporter: How does this postscript remind readers that the legend has passed from teller to teller? What should a historian take from that?

prompt_by_role_plain.investigator: The storyteller doesn't believe half of his story. Which half, the ghost or the trick? Use evidence.
prompt_by_role_plain.attorney: Why does the story end with the teller doubting it? How does that change your story?
prompt_by_role_plain.reporter: How does the ending show the legend was passed from person to person? What should a historian learn?

benchmark.description: Narrative writing (grade-specific wording shown by grade)

prompt_by_role.investigator: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your case account that use the storyteller's doubt to close your account with an honest statement of what remains unknown.
prompt_by_role.attorney: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your feature story that use the storyteller's doubt to end your feature story.
prompt_by_role.reporter: Choose a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view) and write one or two sentences for your town history that use the storyteller's doubt to show your readers that a legend is retold, not recorded.

prompt_by_role_plain.investigator: Pick a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your case account that use the storyteller's doubt to end with what is still unknown.
prompt_by_role_plain.attorney: Pick a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your feature story that use the storyteller's doubt to end your story.
prompt_by_role_plain.reporter: Pick a technique (description, dialogue, pacing, suspense, or point of view). Write one or two sentences for your town history that use the storyteller's doubt to show that a legend is retold, not written down as fact.

recall_checks: Which objects were found near the bridge?
Which belongings were inside Ichabod’s bundle?
What did Ichabod imagine while he ate at the Van Tassel feast?
What did Brom Bones claim happened when he raced the Headless Horseman?
What did Ichabod think he saw at Major André's tree, and what was it really?
What happened to Hans Van Ripper's saddle during the chase?
What news did the old farmer bring back from New York?
How did Brom Bones act whenever someone mentioned the pumpkin?

real_world_connection.prompt: When can a local story become a legend, and what evidence can still be checked?

prompt_by_role.investigator: Write a narrative of the search that separates what the town saw from what it believes.
prompt_by_role.attorney: Write a trial narrative that weighs the ghost story against a possible human motive.
prompt_by_role.reporter: Write a feature story that shows how the disappearance became a local legend.

requirements: Anchor an inference in a textual detail.
Distinguish what is observed from what is reported or claimed.
Shape the account for your role and audience.

levels.descriptor: Uses precise details and explains how they support the account.
Uses relevant details and gives a clear explanation.
Includes a detail but its connection is unclear.
Offers a claim with little textual support.
Uses purposeful pacing, perspective, and detail.
Uses clear structure and a fitting voice.
Has an uneven sequence or voice.

dok4_extension.prompt: Over more than one sitting, write the night of the ride twice: once as the old country wives would tell it by the fire, and once as someone who suspects Brom Bones might tell it. Then explain which details in the text support each version and why Irving never settles the question.
requirements: Write both versions using events and details from the text.
Label each detail as observed, reported, or claimed.
Explain how the narrator's doubt and the gaps in the story keep both versions possible.
